prompt: A word-lookup service stores lowercase English words in a trie whose nodes each hold an **array of 26 child pointers**. It has about a million nodes, and memory profiling shows about 200 MB in the child arrays alone, almost all of it null pointers. Which change attacks the cause most directly?

options.text: Store only the children that exist, in a small map or sorted list, and compress single-child chains
options.explanation: Correct. A tree of N nodes has only N − 1 child links, so about 25 of every 26 array slots are empty. Storing only real children removes that waste, and compressing chains (a radix tree) also removes most of the nodes.

options.text: Widen each node to 256 slots so that any byte can be stored
options.explanation: That makes each node about ten times bigger, and nearly all the new slots would also be empty.
Halving each slot halves the waste but leaves the cause: each node still reserves 26 slots when it typically uses one.

options.text: Add an end-of-word flag to each node
options.explanation: Tries already need that flag to tell words from prefixes. It adds a little memory and does nothing about empty child slots.

workedExample:
1. Each node reserves 26 pointer slots, 208 bytes with 8-byte pointers, so a million nodes need about 208 MB for the arrays, whatever words are stored.
2. A tree of N nodes has exactly N − 1 parent-child links. Spread over 26 slots per node, only about one slot in 26 can ever be used.
3. So the cost comes from reserving slots for children that do not exist. The direct fix is to store only real children: a small hash map or a sorted list of (character, child) pairs.
4. Many trie nodes also sit on single-child chains (unshared word endings). A radix tree merges those chains into labelled edges, cutting the node count as well.

Smaller pointers or adding flags only change constants; they keep reserving space for the 25 missing children.

prompt: You need to store one million independent, approximately uniform SHA-256 values (64 hex characters each) and test membership. A colleague suggests a character trie "because tries are fast for strings". What is the main problem with that plan, and what should you use instead?

options.text: None: the trie stores one node per key, so it is as compact as a hash set
options.explanation: A trie stores one node per distinct prefix, not per key. Random hashes share almost nothing beyond the first few characters, so each key needs its own long chain.

options.text: The trie can hold only 64 nodes, one per character position, so most keys will not fit
options.explanation: Nodes are per distinct *prefix*, not per position. There are millions of different prefixes after just a few characters.

options.text: Random hashes stop sharing prefixes after about 5 to 7 characters, so each key needs a private chain of nearly 60 nodes, about 60 million in total; use a hash set
options.explanation: Correct. With 16 choices per character, the number of possible prefixes passes a million at depth 5, and by depth 7 almost every key is alone. The rest of each hash becomes a single-child chain. A hash set stores each key once and answers exact membership directly.

options.text: Tries cannot store hexadecimal digits, only letters
options.explanation: A trie can use any alphabet; a hex trie simply has up to 16 children per node.

workedExample:
1. Each extra hex character multiplies the possible prefixes by 16. At depth 5 there are just over a million possible prefixes, about one per key, so many keys still share a path: only about 39 % are alone there.
2. By depth 7 there are about 268 million possible prefixes and about 99.6 % of keys have a path to themselves.
3. From there to character 64, each key's remaining characters form a private chain of single-child nodes. Adding up the expected distinct prefixes at every depth gives about 60 million nodes, roughly 60 per key.
4. Exact membership with no prefix queries does not need a trie at all: a hash set stores each key once (or a Bloom filter, if false positives are acceptable). A radix tree would also collapse the chains, with different memory and update trade-offs that would need measuring.
